overview: The Funj Sultanate ruled from Sennar in present-day Sudan. Local centres within its sphere kept distinct institutions. Excavated households at Old Dongola reveal everyday work in a northern community.

periods.title: Before the conventional founding date
periods.summary: The map begins earlier than the sultanate’s conventional founding around 1504. Traditions about earlier Funj origins and movements remain debated; archaeological interpretations do not establish a single certain ancestral homeland.

periods.title: Sennar and its regional centres
periods.summary: Sennar became the capital of the Funj Sultanate. Northern centres such as Old Dongola retained local rulers within its wider sphere. Excavated sixteenth- and seventeenth-century homes reveal work, storage and shared domestic space.

periods.title: Changing power within the sultanate
periods.summary: Royal authority faced internal conflicts. Badi IV was removed in 1762, and powerful hereditary ministers increasingly constrained the sultans. Political struggles preceded the conquest of 1821.

periods.title: After independent Funj rule
periods.summary: Turco-Egyptian forces conquered the sultanate in 1821. This ended its independence, rather than erasing the people and settlements of the region.

periods.title: Recovering everyday history
periods.summary: Modern investigations combine excavation with magnetic survey and ground-penetrating radar. These methods trace buried buildings and help reconstruct the layout of Funj-period Old Dongola.

items.text: In sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Old Dongola, some dwellings shared a courtyard. One excavated compound grouped four homes around the same open space. Builders used sun-dried bricks or frameworks of twigs covered with mud. Shared access helps archaeologists study relationships between neighbours, although it cannot establish exactly how every household was related.

Dongola’s courtyards contained grinding stones, hearths and storage vessels. Plant samples included sorghum and wheat. Together, these finds place food preparation in the open spaces around homes. Grinding grain was part of making a meal, not just a task represented in a royal account. The evidence does not supply a complete menu or identify every cook.

A deposit in room U50 at Old Dongola contained storage pots standing on woven mats, with some covered by basketry lids or reused bowls. The deposit dates to roughly the late sixteenth or early seventeenth century. These objects preserve a practical system for storing things, including an economical second job for an old bowl.

One rectangular basket in that deposit held a small pot with a basketry cover, a wooden key, a grinding stone and two spindle whorls. These finds bring household equipment into view together. The key survived; what it opened is less certain. Objects found together do not necessarily all belong to one task.

The traveller Evliya Çelebi reported six schools at Dongola in 1672/1673. A modern archaeological study compares that written account with a survey that could not clearly identify the reported religious buildings. The account is evidence for educational activity, but its numbers are not a verified count of excavated classrooms or of children attending lessons.

An Arabic order from Old Dongola, studied in 2026, instructs a man named Khidr to arrange exchanges involving goods interpreted as textiles and a ewe with her young. It names King Qashqash and his scribe Hamad. The document, dated broadly to the sixteenth or seventeenth century, shows government handling material transactions. Some commodity names remain difficult to read.

The royal order uses both sides of an irregular piece of paper. The reverse adds further instructions, probably concerning cotton cloth or headwear. Scholars distinguish the readable names and commands from damaged or ambiguous words. A small piece of paperwork can reveal people who are scarcely visible in grand political histories, without settling every detail of their lives.

Chemical analysis of seventeen wool, cotton and silk samples from seventeenth- and eighteenth-century Dongola identified dyes from plants and animals. The researchers distinguished fabrics they considered local from imported textiles. Small scraps can therefore reveal choices about colour and connections beyond the city, even when the original garment has disappeared.

The same study identified kermes and lac colourants, made from insects, alongside plant dyes. One crimson knitted wool fragment was interpreted as part of a fez. Getting dressed could involve surprisingly varied raw materials. The possible hat identification remains an interpretation of a fragment, not a complete surviving wardrobe.

Seeds identified as tobacco were recovered at Old Dongola and dated approximately to 1664 to 1760. Their presence supports research into local cultivation and changing habits. The study treats the exact timing and route of tobacco’s arrival as uncertain. This is evidence of a historical practice, rather than proof that every household grew or used the plant.

A 2025 study of excavated pottery at Sennar and Al Khandaq found differences in production. Handmade forms with relatively simple decoration were prominent at Sennar, while the Al Khandaq material included wheel-made wares and more varied surface treatments. Comparing the two places shows local choices continuing within a connected region; one technique does not rank an entire community’s skill.

In a 2026 account of the Dongola research, the University of Warsaw describes local residents as partners who exchange knowledge with archaeologists. Residents still use a name meaning the King’s House for a building studied by the team. Such remembered names can guide questions about a place, while excavated documents provide a different kind of evidence.

ending.text: Turco-Egyptian forces conquered the Funj Sultanate in 1821 after prolonged internal struggles. Its independent government ended, while communities and their local histories continued. The map’s separate endpoints in 1530 and 1815 do not mark two destructions of the sultanate.
